intro.html: Humor comes in many flavors. Some is warm and clever, some is dry and quiet, and some has teeth. Writers choose their humor words carefully, because the word tells you how the joke lands: a witty remark delights, a sarcastic one stings.

Gentle and clever: witty, wry, droll, levity. Out of place: facetious (joking when you should be serious). Sharp: sarcastic, sardonic. Kinds of mockery: a satire exposes foolishness, a parody imitates and exaggerates, and to lampoon is to make fun of someone in public.
When you meet one of these words in a passage, ask: Is the humor kind or cutting? Is it suited to the moment? Is it aimed at someone?

words.def: cleverly funny, especially with quick remarks
words.ex: Her {witty} reply made even the grumpy bus driver laugh.
words.ctx: Grandpa’s toasts were never long or dull; they were {witty}, full of quick, clever lines that had the whole room laughing.
words.etym: From Old English witig, “clever, wise,” from wit (mind, understanding).

mn.text: Rosa always has a quick, clever line ready, and her friends can’t stop laughing: she is {witty}.

scene.alt: A teen girl tells a clever joke and her friends burst out laughing.

words.def: dryly funny, often with a touch of irony
words.ex: Dad gave a {wry} smile when our “waterproof” tent leaked on the first night.
words.ctx: Instead of complaining about the canceled flight, Aunt Lin made a {wry} joke: at least the airport chairs were teaching her patience.
words.etym: From Old English wrigian, “to turn,” so first meaning twisted to one side, as in a crooked, wry smile.

mn.text: Rain pours on the picnic, and Grandpa Gus gives a crooked half smile: “Lovely day… for ducks.” His humor is {wry}.

scene.alt: In the pouring rain, a grandfather with an umbrella smiles a crooked smile while a duck splashes happily.

words.def: funny in an odd, quiet or dry way
words.ex: The old fisherman had a {droll} way of telling stories, never smiling while everyone else laughed.
words.ctx: The comedian was not loud or silly but {droll}; he spoke in a flat, quiet voice and let the oddness of his remarks do the rest.

mn.text: Baker Omar gives a bread roll a mustache and, with a perfectly straight face, bows: “Sir Roll, at your service.” His joke is {droll}.

scene.alt: A baker with a straight face presents a bread roll as if it were a knight, and a girl giggles.

words.def: lightness of mood or humor, especially at a serious time
words.ex: A little {levity} helped the nervous players relax before the final game.
words.ctx: The ceremony was solemn, and the principal frowned at any {levity}; even a giggle from the back row earned a stern look.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

words.etym: From Latin levitas, “lightness,” from levis (light in weight).
words.note: Levity can be welcome (it eases a tense room) or unwelcome (it seems disrespectful); the sentence tells you which.

mn.cue: LEV = LIGHT: a joke that LEVitates
mn.text: The long meeting feels heavy until Dev’s joke floats up like a balloon and lifts everyone’s mood: a moment of {levity}.

scene.alt: In an office meeting, a young man’s joke floats up like a balloon and his coworkers laugh.

words.def: joking at a time that calls for being serious
words.ex: “Maybe we should all move to the moon,” Kai said, but he was only being {facetious}.
words.ctx: When the coach asked how to fix the team’s defense, Jonah’s {facetious} answer, “Hire a dragon,” got laughs but no thanks; the coach wanted a real plan.
words.etym: From French facétieux, from Latin facetia, “a jest, a witty saying.”

mn.cue: FACE-tious: a silly FACE at the wrong time
mn.text: When the teacher asks why his homework is late, Pip pulls a silly face and says, “My goldfish needed it.” He is being {facetious}.

scene.alt: A stern teacher asks for homework, and a boy makes a silly face and jokes.

words.def: saying the opposite of what one means, to mock or show annoyance
words.ex: “Oh, great, more homework,” Lila said in a {sarcastic} voice.
words.ctx: When Dev called the three-hour traffic jam “a delightful little drive,” no one was fooled; his tone was {sarcastic}, and everyone knew he was miserable.
words.etym: From sarcasm, from Greek sarkazein, “to tear flesh,” and so “to sneer, to speak bitterly,” from sarx (flesh).

mn.text: The bus splashes Kai with mud, and he says, “Oh, wonderful. Just what I wanted.” He means the opposite: he is being {sarcastic}.

scene.alt: A bus splashes a boy with puddle water, and he flatly says, “Oh, great.”

words.ex: The tired reporter gave a {sardonic} laugh when the “quick” meeting entered its third hour.
words.ctx: After years of broken promises from the landlord about fixing the heat, Mr. Felix greeted the newest promise with a {sardonic} grin, as if to say he would believe it when he felt it.
words.etym: From Greek sardonios, used of bitter, scornful laughter.

mn.cue: SARDINE-ic: a grim grin, packed like SARDINES
mn.text: Squashed into the train like a sardine in a can, Felix gives a grim grin: “Plenty of room, eh?” His humor is {sardonic}.

scene.alt: Four commuters are squashed together on a train platform; one gives a grim, mocking grin.

words.def: humor that exposes foolishness or wrongdoing, often by exaggerating it
words.ex: The comic strip is a gentle {satire} of office life, full of pointless meetings.
words.ctx: The novel is more than a funny story; it is a {satire} that uses exaggeration to show how silly the town’s obsession with perfect lawns has become.
words.etym: From Latin satura, “a mixture,” the name of a kind of Roman poem that made fun of people’s faults.

mn.cue: SAT + IRE: anger turned into laughs
mn.text: Tired of silly rules, the students put their ire into a play about a king who bans frowning; the whole school laughs and gets the point. The play is a {satire}.

scene.alt: On a stage, a boy dressed as a silly king orders “No frowning!” while two classmates laugh.

words.def: a funny imitation that exaggerates the original
words.ex: The class wrote a {parody} of a weather report, forecasting a ninety percent chance of homework.
words.ctx: The song was not original; it was a {parody} of a well-known lullaby, with the same tune but new, silly words about a cat who refuses to go to sleep.
words.etym: From Greek paroidia, “a song sung beside another”: para (beside) + oide (song).

mn.text: The parrot copies Grandpa’s sneeze, only louder and sillier: “AH-AH-AH-CHOOOO!” It is a {parody} of his sneeze.

scene.alt: A grandfather sneezes, and his parrot copies the sneeze much louder and sillier.

words.def: to mock in public, often in writing or pictures
words.ex: The comedy show {lampooned} the strangest fashion trends of the year.
words.ctx: The cartoonist loved to {lampoon} show-offs; in her strips, anyone who bragged soon had a pigeon land on his hat in front of a crowd.

mn.cue: a joke poster under the LAMP
mn.text: The town is tired of Sir Rex’s bragging, so someone hangs a funny poster under the street lamp: “SIR BRAGS-A-LOT.” It {lampoons} him for all to see.

labels.text: a joke poster under the LAMP

scene.alt: Children laugh at a joke banner about a bragging knight hung under a street lamp, while the knight fumes.

how it feels

after.html: A parody always copies something: a song, a movie, a style. A satire may or may not copy anything; its aim is to show that some behavior is foolish. Many satires use parody as a tool. To lampoon is the action: to mock someone in public, often through satire or parody.

after.name: vo-cloze

opts.s: The serious ceremony left no room for {levity}; even the youngest children sat silent.

after.cap: Lightness of mood at a serious time is levity; its opposite is gravity.

items.q: Stuck in the rain without an umbrella, Dev says, “Perfect weather for a walk!” He is being…
items.why: He says the opposite of what he means, to show annoyance: that is sarcasm.

items.q: A school video copies the style of a nature documentary, but it follows the class hamster as if it were a lion. It is a…
items.why: It imitates the documentary style and exaggerates it for laughs: a parody.

items.q: True or false: a facetious remark is a serious, thoughtful answer.
items.why: False. A facetious remark is a joke made when a serious answer was expected.

items.q: Which word best fits a grim, scornful smile?
items.why: Sardonic humor is grim and scornful. Droll and witty are friendlier kinds of funny, and facetious means joking at the wrong time.
